title: Prolonged insular isolation and mosaic cranial divergence in Haplomylomys
content:
Abstract
Insular systems provide valuable opportunities to examine morphological divergence under contrasting histories of isolation. This study evaluated cranial size and shape variation among insular taxa of Haplomylomys from northwestern Mexico, with emphasis on differences between older and recent insular lineages and on the potential role of craniofacial evolutionary allometry (CREA). A total of 179 adult specimens were analysed using two-dimensional geometric morphometrics of dorsal and lateral cranial views at both species and population levels. Principal component, canonical variate, Procrustes ANOVA, and allometric regression analyses were used to assess patterns of shape variation, group differentiation, and covariation between size and shape. The rostrum consistently showed the strongest signal of morphological divergence, whereas the braincase showed intermediate differentiation and the cranium as a whole showed greater overlap. Older insular lineage taxa occupied more discrete positions in morphospace than recent insular lineage taxa. Although size and shape covaried significantly, allometry explained only a small fraction of total shape variation. Associations between cranial proportions and island area were weak and did not differ between lineages. These results indicate that cranial diversification in insular Haplomylomys is associated more strongly with prolonged isolation than with a shared allometric trajectory.
